title: Mary Emma Cuffee Bunn
summary: Mary Emma Cuffee Bunn (1847–1937) was a Shinnecock woman whose life connected language-bearing family knowledge, maritime labor, survival after the Circassian disaster, education, and intergenerational community continuity.
content:
Mary Emma Cuffee Bunn (1847–1937) was a Shinnecock woman whose ninety-year life connected language-bearing family knowledge, maritime labor, the losses of the Circassian disaster, and the education and public service of the next generation. She was born on July 6, 1847, to Agee Cuffee and Mary Ann Cuffee, whose knowledge of the Shinnecock language was documented by later researchers.1

Family, language, and maritime life

Mary Emma grew up within a Shinnecock family whose history carried language, church, work, and community memory across generations. She married David Waukus Bunn, a Shinnecock mariner and whaler, and they raised Charles Sumner Bunn, Oscar Smith Bunn, and Mabel Bunn on the reservation.2

David’s work belonged to a much larger Shinnecock maritime history. Whaling and shipboard labor created skill, income, and far-reaching experience, but it also exposed Shinnecock families to dangerous working conditions and long absences. Family history therefore cannot be told only through the men listed on crew records; it also depends on the women who held households and kinship networks together.

The Circassian loss

On December 30, 1876, David Waukus Bunn and nine other Shinnecock men died while working aboard the grounded cargo ship Circassian off Mecox Bay. Mary Emma was twenty-nine and was left to raise three children. Shinnecock family accounts remember her mother meeting the first shock of the news with a short insistence that grief and necessary work would have to exist together: “There’s work to be done.”3

Lois Marie Hunter later wrote that Mary Emma raised and educated her children after the disaster. Her son Charles Sumner Bunn attended the New York State Normal School at New Paltz and became known as a guide, decoy carver, church elder, and Shinnecock trustee. That sequence makes the family’s endurance visible without reducing Mary Emma to widowhood alone.4

Community continuity

In 1915, Mary Emma was photographed at a Shinnecock Reservation powwow with women whose families had also lived through the Circassian loss. The photograph records presence decades after newspapers and local histories had wrongly used the disaster to promote a “vanishing Indian” story. Mary Emma lived until December 7, 1937.5

Reading the sources carefully

Some nineteenth- and early twentieth-century sources describe Shinnecock families through racist ideas about blood, racial “purity,” or disappearance. Those claims do not define Mary Emma or the Shinnecock Nation. They are evidence of the colonial frameworks imposed by outside writers. Her biography is better understood through kinship, survival after labor catastrophe, education, artistry, and continued Shinnecock community life.

References

  • Beverly Jensen, Shinnecock Indian Nation (2015), pp. 87–93.
  • Nancy Shoemaker, ed., Living with Whales: Documents and Oral Histories of Native New England Whaling History (2014), p. 117.
  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History (1983), pp. 321 and 397.
  • John A. Strong, We Are Still Here! The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island Today, p. 36.
  • Shinnecock Indian Nation Ancestors from 19th and 20th Century, p. 4.
why_this_matters: Mary Emma Cuffee Bunn’s life centers the work Shinnecock women carried through maritime loss: sustaining families, educating children, protecting kinship, and refusing the false claim that catastrophe made the community disappear.
